opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think that threshold is where things really change, and the reason is that the main thing it automates is the work of building better AI.

Right now automation is bottlenecked by human labor at every step. Humans figure out what to automate, design the systems, run the experiments, write the code, and integrate it into businesses. Progress moves at roughly the speed of human researchers and engineers. Once you have AI that beats top experts at basically anything done on a computer, that includes ML research, chip design, and software engineering. So the inputs to AI progress start getting automated, and you get a feedback loop. Better AI makes AI research faster, which produces better AI.

You also aren't limited by how many top researchers exist anymore. You might have a few thousand world-class ML researchers today. With compute, you could run the equivalent of hundreds of thousands or millions of them, working around the clock and possibly faster than humans think. Even if each one is only modestly better than the best humans, that's a huge increase in effective research effort. I'd expect years of progress to start compressing into months.

Then it spills over. If AI is that good at computer-based work, it's also very good at designing robots, writing control software, and running simulations. The physical world is slower, since you have to build factories and run experiments, but those bottlenecks get attacked by vastly more cognitive labor than we've ever had. So I'd expect a fairly sharp transition. First, rapid automation of knowledge work and AI R&D itself, then a push into physical automation that could happen much faster than past technological transitions.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty. Compute could limit things, and so could the need for real-world experiments or regulation and adoption friction. But I think the default expectation should be that the pace speeds up a lot once we cross that line, not that it continues on the current trend. That's a big part of why I think it's worth preparing now, before we're in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: The response predicts faster progress after the capability threshold, but gives no arrival date or early-2030s forecast.

r002.rationale: It says AI could design robots and that physical bottlenecks would be attacked with more cognitive labor, but does not identify human physical labor as a way for AI to bootstrap its robotic capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AI research feedback loops and robot design, but does not attribute robotics progress to the model-and-data scaling approach used for cognitive AI.

r004.rationale: It describes a later push into physical automation, but gives no one-to-two-year timeframe or claim that AI-controlled systems could complete the production loop for building and maintaining more AI systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's going to be much more uneven and much more jagged than people often picture. The mental image a lot of folks have is something like a switch flipping: one day you have systems that can do everything a top expert does at a computer, and the next day the economy is completely transformed. And I think that gets both halves wrong.

The first thing to say is that "outperforms top experts at computer-based work" is doing a lot of load-bearing work in that question. In practice, what I expect is that capability shows up domain by domain, and within domains it shows up task by task. You already see this now, right? Models are great at some fairly narrow slices of software engineering and still fumble on things that a mid-level engineer would find trivial, like keeping a coherent picture of a large codebase over a long project or knowing when a requirement is secretly ambiguous. So even when the headline capability arrives, I expect there'll be this long tail of things that aren't quite covered, and those gaps matter a lot for whether you can actually remove the human from the loop.

The second thing is that the bottleneck on automation is often not capability at all. It's integration, it's trust, it's liability, it's regulatory structure, it's just the sheer organizational slowness of companies figuring out how to restructure their workflows. Think about how long it took for electricity to actually change factory layouts after it was available. The technology was there for decades before people redesigned the production line around it. I don't think AI will take decades, because the AI itself can help with a lot of that integration work, which is a genuinely new feature of this technology. But I do think the diffusion lag is real and people underrate it.

That said, I want to be careful not to swing too far toward "it'll all be gradual and fine." Because there's one domain where I think the acceleration could be really sharp, and that's AI research itself. If you have systems that are better than the best human researchers at the computer-based parts of AI development, which is most of it, then you get this feedback loop where the thing being automated is the thing that makes the next version better. That's where I think the pace could go from "fast but legible" to something that's genuinely hard for institutions to keep up with. And the reason that matters is that it's the one place where the usual diffusion lag doesn't protect you, because the AI labs are the ones most motivated and most able to deploy the systems internally right away.

So my overall picture is something like: in the broad economy, faster than most economists expect but slower than the most breathless forecasts, with a lot of bumpiness and a lot of sectors where the humans stay in the loop for reasons that have nothing to do with raw capability. And then inside the frontier labs, potentially a very rapid compounding dynamic that could outrun everyone's ability to understand what's happening. And honestly, that second piece is the one I lose sleep over, because that's where the governance and safety questions get hardest, and it's happening in the part of the world with the least external visibility.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect it to make the pace of automation much faster, because you’re automating a lot of the work that goes into further automation. Today, if you want to automate a task, you need people to understand the workflow, build the software, test it, and figure out how to deploy it. If AI can do all of that better than the best human experts, you can have many copies of those systems working on many different tasks at once.

The particularly consequential case is AI research itself. If these systems can improve the algorithms and software that power the next generation of AI, you get a feedback loop: better AI makes progress on AI faster, which produces still better AI. That could make the transition from systems that are roughly human-level to systems that are much more capable quite compressed.

That doesn’t mean everything in the economy gets automated overnight. Physical work still requires robots and infrastructure, and adoption can be slowed by organizational changes, regulation, and the need to establish reliability. But I’d distinguish those deployment bottlenecks from the pace of technological progress. Once you can automate the cognitive work of developing and deploying automation, I’d expect that technological frontier to move very quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect that to be a pretty dramatic acceleration, because you’re automating the process of figuring out how to automate things. Today, even when a task is technically possible to automate, someone has to identify the opportunity, build the software, test it, and integrate it into an organization. All of that takes scarce human time.

If you have AI that’s better than top human experts at computer-based work, you can potentially run many copies of it doing that work in parallel. And some of those copies can work on improving AI itself, which could accelerate the process further.

That doesn’t mean everything in the economy changes overnight. Physical infrastructure, manufacturing, regulation, and organizational adoption can still take time. But I’d expect the pace of automation to become much less constrained by the availability of people who can develop and deploy it, and that could make the transition much faster than people are used to.
